quotes.text: They produced a distinctive soft musical style, combining Karen's contralto vocals with Richard's harmonizing, arranging, and composition.

The duo's brand of melodic pop produced a record-breaking run of hit recordings on the American Top 40 and Adult Contemporary charts, and they became leading sellers in the soft rock, easy listening, and adult contemporary music genres.

He was asked to be the organist for weddings and services at the local Methodist church; instead of playing traditional hymns, he would sometimes rearrange contemporary Beatles songs in a "church" style.
Richard led the group and wrote all the arrangements, and they began to rehearse daily.
Karen and Richard were close, and shared a common interest in music. In particular, they became fans of Les Paul and Mary Ford, whose music featured multiple overdubbed voices and instruments.
As Carpenters, she and brother Richard, a musical genius in a league all this own, created timeless music beloved by fans of all ages, all races, all backgrounds.

Back then, Karen and Richard were often thought of- if at all- as singles artists by the rock elite. The more carefully examined truth was that under Richard's impeccable leadership, he and his sister created beautifully crafted albums, each distinct and unlike the ones before or after.

Ticket shows how Richard can brilliantly reimagine records by others, and Karen hits vocal pay dirt by giving us a delicate "All of My Life". Their jazz roots come into play here as does their background and love for choral music.
The debut is good but not great- yet the stage was set.
The album cover is terrific, but for the most part, the music contained is so stiffly close to the original hits in execution that I'd rather just listen to their superior studio work.
The best part about Live in Japan? It reveals that even without any technical wizardry, Karen was a one of a kind vocalist. She was just as good in person as she was behind a studio microphone.
You put great stock behind originality, innovation, and rawness, all of which the Carpenters consciously avoid.
While I love their music, I think their insistence on sticking to the easy listening sound was detrimental.
There are some songs ("All You Get From Love Is A Love Song" immediately comes to mind) where you can hear Karen's pain and other MOR-unfriendly emotions creep out a bit.
I think the Carpenters definitely DON'T rock!

"Offering / Ticket to Ride" - 1969 album. Varied in style and approach. The disc has a very 60's rock / pop sound... Super ambitious. Karen's voice has flashes of what we've come to expect. The album is much different than their breakout hits and romantic sounds that came in the following decade.
"Made in America" – Their 1981 "comeback" album. They were striving for a hit, and it unfortunately shows. Seems stripped of the ambition mentioned above... Richard's arrangements rule.
"Passage"- Daring 1977 album. Totally unexpected in every way. Bold and sassy. Confident. Each cut is very different than the one before.
"Horizon"- Best visual presentation of Karen and Richard as real people. Ultra polished collection but with real backbone, Elegant, classy, best recorded sound of Karen's voice ever.
"Close to You"- Back to the top of my rankings. The album that cemented my love affair with Karen's voice. Fresh. Energetic. Brilliant in every way.
Varied styles affirm their ability to serve any genre well.
